nameStory: The Beaverpond Clubtail gets its name from two key features: its preferred habitat around beaver ponds and wetlands, and its distinctive 'clubbed' tail tip that widens dramatically at the end. Like all clubtail dragonflies, the males have an enlarged segment at the tip of their abdomen that resembles a wooden club or paddle.
description: The Beaverpond Clubtail is a medium-sized dragonfly with the characteristic clubbed tail that gives this family its name. These skilled aerial hunters have large compound eyes, four strong wings that they hold perpendicular to their body when resting, and a long abdomen with distinctive black and yellow markings. Adults typically measure about 2-2.5 inches long with a wingspan reaching nearly 3 inches. They're most active during warm, sunny days when they patrol their territory with swift, darting flight patterns.

idTips.label: Clubbed tail tip
idTips.description: The male's abdomen ends in a noticeably swollen, club-like segment that's much wider than the rest of the tail - like a baseball bat or paddle handle ending in a bulb

idTips.label: Eye placement
idTips.description: Large compound eyes are separated and don't touch at the top of the head, unlike darner dragonflies - you can see a clear gap between them when viewed from the front

idTips.label: Resting position
idTips.description: Wings stick straight out from the sides of the body when perched, never folded back along the abdomen like damselflies do

idTips.label: Body coloration
idTips.description: Black abdomen with bright yellow stripes and spots, particularly noticeable on the sides - the pattern looks freshly painted in good light

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Strong, direct flight with sudden stops and hovering - they patrol back and forth over water with confident, purposeful movements

habitat: Look for Beaverpond Clubtails around slow-moving or still freshwater habitats, especially beaver ponds, marshes, and the quiet backwaters of streams and rivers. They prefer areas with muddy or silty bottoms where their larvae can burrow, often in spots with emergent vegetation like cattails and sedges. In New England, they're most common at lower elevations in wooded areas where beavers have created or modified wetland systems.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from their aquatic larval stage in late spring, usually May into early June. Look for fresh exoskeletons (exuvia) clinging to vegetation near the water's edge.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs from June through August when adults are actively hunting, mating, and laying eggs. This is the best time to observe their territorial patrolling behavior over water.
seasonality.fall: Activity decreases significantly by September as adults complete their life cycle. Late-emerging individuals may still be seen in early fall during warm weather.
seasonality.winter: Adults are absent during winter months. Larvae continue developing underwater in the mud and sediment, surviving freezing temperatures until spring emergence.

funFact: Beaverpond Clubtail larvae are underground architects that can spend 2-4 years buried in pond sediment before emerging as adults - they're like aquatic moles with gills, using their powerful legs to dig through mud while hunting other insects with lightning-fast extendable jaws.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other clubtail species, but the Beaverpond Clubtail's preference for still waters helps distinguish it from the Rapids Clubtail (which loves fast-flowing streams) and the Lancet Clubtail (found in larger rivers). Memory trick: 'Beaverpond' = still, quiet water where beavers would actually build.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific genus name recently changed from Gomphus to Phanogomphus based on genetic studies, so older field guides may list this species under a different scientific name. This name shuffle is common in dragonfly identification as scientists better understand evolutionary relationships.
compareHints: Among its Phanogomphus relatives in New England, the Beaverpond Clubtail is most reliably identified by habitat - it strongly prefers beaver ponds and similar still waters over the flowing streams favored by Rapids and Lancet Clubtails. The Dusky and Ashy Clubtails are less common and have subtly different coloration patterns, while the Harpoon Clubtail has a more distinctively shaped club.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Phanogomphus relatives, the lancet clubtail is distinguished by its bright green thorax stripes and green triangular abdominal markings.
Among its Phanogomphus relatives, the dusky clubtail lives up to its name with more subdued coloration than the bright yellow Rapids Clubtail or the pale Ashy Clubtail.

Among its Phanogomphus cousins, the Ashy Clubtail is distinguished by its pale coloration — the Dusky Clubtail is much darker, the Rapids Clubtail has more distinct yellow markings, and the Lancet Clubtail is smaller and more delicately built.
Among its Phanogomphus relatives in New England, the harpoon clubtail is distinguished by its specific tail appendage shape and the pattern of yellow markings on its thorax.
